About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Agricultural and Horticultural
Science Years 12–13 of the New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga
o Aotearoa is being published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Agricultural and Horticultural Science Years
12–13 is still in development. Once that is completed, Agricultural and Horticultural
Science Years 12–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as a
National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training
Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Agricultural and Horticultural Science Years 12–13 will be required to start
using it in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Through the study of Agricultural and Horticultural Science, students are taught to
apply and extend knowledge of biological, environmental, physical, technological, and
management systems. They investigate how plant, animal, soil, environmental, and
production systems interact, and how management decisions influence productivity,
profitability, sustainability, and environmental outcomes. Students use scientific
knowledge, observations, data, and evidence to explain production outcomes,
evaluate management practices, and solve problems within agricultural and
horticultural contexts.

Agricultural and Horticultural Science provides students with the knowledge and
practices to analyse production systems, evaluate evidence, and make informed
decisions about the management of plants, animals, land, water, and resources.
Students develop the ability to investigate biological processes, assess production
opportunities and challenges, and communicate evidence-based recommendations
using appropriate disciplinary concepts and terminology.

As students progress through Years 12–13 Agricultural and Horticultural Science,
they are supported to develop their understanding of scientific concepts, production
systems, management practices, and disciplinary language. This enables students to
communicate reasoning and decision-making using evidence, data, scientific
principles, and system-wide perspectives.

Agricultural and Horticultural Science | Years 12–13 | October 2026                                                                                                                  Page 6

Nature of science
Science is a way of testing theories of natural phenomena using evidence and
reasoning. In science, theories and explanations can be supported by careful
observation, measurement, and experiment, and they change when new evidence is
discovered.

Science is a collaborative human activity that develops knowledge of the natural
world. This knowledge enables scientists to create technologies, inventions, and
innovations that benefit society and help solve problems. Because scientific
knowledge can have both positive and negative impacts, it must be applied
responsibly. In New Zealand, science is closely connected to kaitiakitanga,
recognising responsibilities of guardianship and care for the natural world. Scientists
communicate their ideas, evidence, and findings so they can be evaluated,
challenged, and used to inform decisions and actions.

Investigating in science

Scientists develop meaningful questions and use investigations to explain
phenomena. They gather or select evidence, collect primary data or source
secondary data, analyse data, identify patterns and relationships, evaluate evidence,
consider alternative explanations, and distinguish between strong and weak support
for claims. Scientists test theories by attempting to disprove them rather than prove
them.

At Years 12 and 13, students continue to investigate scientific questions, gather and
analyse evidence, and use this evidence to explain scientific phenomena and develop
their understanding of Agricultural and Horticultural Science.

Opportunities should be provided each year for students to undertake both practical
and secondary-source investigations, working independently and collaboratively.

Contexts and investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and
interests of students, their community, and the local environment.

Delivery of Agricultural and Horticultural Science programme must align with Safety
and Science guidance.

Further guidance on programme design, investigation opportunities, and resource
selection is available in the Agricultural and Horticultural Science Curriculum Support
Document

                          Soil temperature is the primary driver of seed germination and root activity.
                          Adequate gas exchange in the soil is essential for root respiration.
                          Low oxygen levels (e.g. in waterlogged soils) can lead to root suffocation and reduced growth.

                         Light
                          Light is an energy source for photosynthesis.
                          Sunshine hours, light intensity, duration (photoperiod), and wavelength all influence plant growth and development.
                         Water
                          Water is essential for plant growth, as it is a reactant for photosynthesis and respiration, transports nutrients, maintains turgor
                           pressure, and supports cellular growth.
                          Evapotranspiration is the combined loss of water from the soil (evaporation) and plants (transpiration) and can vary according to
                           factors (e.g. wind speed, temperature, leaf area).
                         Temperature
                          Temperature affects the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions, including photosynthesis and respiration.
                          Each plant species has an optimum temperature range for growth.
                          Temperature influences germination, flowering, and fruit development.
                          Growing degree days (GDD) are a cumulative measurement of heat used by growers to predict the development rates of plants.
                          Dormancy is a period when seeds or plants stop growing to survive unfavourable conditions. Growth resumes when conditions
                           improve.
                          Vernalisation is a period of cold weather that some plants need before they can flower and reproduce.
                          Chill requirement, typically hours between 0°C and 7°C, is the amount of winter cold a fruit tree needs to break dormancy and
                           produce normal flowering and fruit set.
                         Frost
                          Frost occurs when the temperature of a surface falls below the freezing point of water (0°C). Cold air is denser than warm air and
                           behaves like a fluid. It flows downhill and settles in low-lying areas, depressions, or behind solid barriers (e.g. dense hedges).
                           These areas are known as frost pockets.
                          Frost can benefit plants by reducing pest and disease populations. This helps meet winter chilling requirements and improves the
                           flavour of some crops by increasing their sugar content.
                          Frost can damage plants by freezing and disrupting plant cells, reducing fruit quality, and destroying flowers, which can lower or
                           prevent crop production.
                         Snow and hail
                          Hail forms inside large storm clouds when water droplets freeze into layers of ice. As the ice stones grow bigger and heavier, they
                           eventually fall rapidly to the ground as hailstones.
                          Snow forms when water vapour freezes into ice crystals in cold air. These crystals join together to form snowflakes, which fall
                           slowly and can create an insulating layer on the ground.
                         Humidity
                          Relative humidity is a measure of how much water vapour is currently in the air compared to the maximum amount of water
                           vapour the air could hold at that specific temperature. It is expressed as a percentage and is a critical factor in both plant
                           transpiration, photosynthesis, and disease status.
                          Humidity affects the rate of transpiration (water loss from stoma).

                           meet plant or pasture needs when rainfall is insufficient.
                          Proper drainage ensures roots have access to oxygen, increases respiration rates, reduces disease risk, and improves nutrient
                           uptake, promoting plant growth and higher yields.
                          Consistent, good quality drinking water is provided to livestock in every paddock through troughs supplied from a range of sources

                          Controlled environments are covered in a material (e.g. glass, polycarbonate, polyethylene film), which determines light

                          Shade cloth is woven synthetic fabric used to reduce light intensity and air temperature.
                          Reflective mulch reflects sunlight back up into the lower canopy of fruit trees or crops, improving fruit colour and discouraging

                          Artificial lighting can be used to extend the photoperiod (day length) or supplement low light in winter.
                          Crop row orientation is the physical direction rows are planted, usually north–south. This helps both sides of the row receive equal
                           sunlight throughout the day.
                          Correct crop spacing balances the need for maximum yield per hectare against the risk of high humidity and disease spread
                           caused by poor airflow between crowded plants.
                          Pasture length is managed to maintain pasture quality and encourage regrowth after grazing.

                         Pruning and training
                          Pruning and training are active physiological interventions used to direct a plant's energy away from unwanted vegetative growth
                           toward high-value, reproductive yield or aesthetic outcomes.
                          Pruning is the strategic removal of a plant parts to improve health and productivity.
                          Root pruning is a technique used to restrict vegetative vigour or prepare a plant for transplanting by cutting back the root system.
                          Stopping is the removal of the terminal or apical bud to break apical dominance. This encourages the plant to branch out laterally,
                           creating a bushier plant.
                          Thinning can be done on leaves, branches, and fruits.
                           o Hand or machine thinning is the precision removal of excess growth or fruitlets to improve light penetration or fruit size.
                           o Chemical thinning is the use of hormones to induce the plant to drop a portion of its fruit, ensuring the remaining crop reaches a
                             premium size.
                         Management of wind
                          Wind can be managed using protected environments (e.g. greenhouses, shade structures), which reduce exposure.
                          Staking and tying is a physical support method used to protect young or unstable plants from wind damage, preventing them from
                           snapping, uprooting, or leaning permanently.
                          Shelter belts are rows of trees or artificial shelter designed to reduce wind speed. By reducing wind, shelter belts lower
                           evapotranspiration rates, prevent physical damage to fruit (e.g. wind rub), and create a warmer microclimate for both plants and
                           livestock.
                         Management of temperature
                          Temperature can be modified using several techniques, including site selection, provision of shelter, and the use of protected
                           environments.
                          A protected environment is a modified space designed to shield plants or processes from outside weather conditions (e.g.
                           greenhouse, cloche, shade house). The use of different cladding, cloths, heating, misting, and ventilation systems allow
                           temperature to be modified for a specific crop.
                         Management of frost
                          Frosts can damage vegetative growth as well as flowers and fruit, with the potential to cause significant damage.
                          Growers use a range of techniques to protect plants from frosts (e.g. frost pots, wind machines, helicopters, overhead sprinklers,
                           covers, structures).
                          Passive frost management practices include row orientation and the planting of crops on north-facing slopes rather than the lower
                           lying basins where cold air accumulates.
                         Management of humidity
                          Intermittent misting is an automated humidity control method that applies a fine spray of water at regular intervals to maintain a
                           thin film of moisture, reducing water loss through transpiration and keeping plant tissues cool.
                          Ventilation helps regulate humidity levels by replacing moist, stagnant air with fresh, drier air, reducing the risk of condensation
                           and fungal diseases.
                          Propagating tents create a highly humid microclimate by trapping moisture around seedlings or cuttings, helping to minimise water
                           loss and support successful plant establishment
                         Management of hail
                          Hail netting is a physical barrier made of high-density polyethylene mesh installed over orchards, vineyards, or high-value crops.
                           The netting is designed to catch hailstones and allow them to roll off or sit on top of the canopy rather than striking the fruit or
                           foliage.
                         Management of carbon dioxide
                          Carbon dioxide enrichment increases CO₂ levels in controlled environments (e.g. greenhouse) above natural concentrations to
                           enhance photosynthesis, promoting faster plant growth and improving yield.
                          Carbon dioxide enrichment is achieved through propane burners or compressed CO₂ from tanks that release CO₂ through a
                           network of plastic tubes with small holes (soaker hoses) positioned near the plant canopy.
                         Management of oxygen
                          High atmospheric oxygen levels are required for healthy plant respiration, especially during the night when plants consume
                           oxygen rather than produce it.
                          Ventilation is the process of exchanging stagnant, oxygen-depleted air inside a growing structure with fresh, oxygen-rich air from
                           the outside. This can be achieved through passive (e.g. opening roof, side vents) or active means (e.g. using exhaust fans).
                          Aeration is the mechanical process of increasing oxygen movement within the soil or other growing media. Techniques (e.g.
                           coring, cultivation, ripping) can be used to increase soil aeration.
